newsitem.title: UK: New paradigm close as natural UK jobless rate dips.
newsitem.headline: New paradigm close as natural UK jobless rate dips.

text.p: The British economy could be on the brink of a new era where fast growth and low unemployment are not accompanied by a surge in inflation, the so-called New Paradigm, economists say.

U.S. Federal reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has said that supply side and technological improvements may have quickened the sustainable growth rate there, engendering the economic equivalent of nirvana and analysts say a similar scenario is within the UK's grasp too.

"It is fascinating that whereas unemployment is down to 5.5 percent there is as yet no major sign that pay settlements are starting to pick up," said Ruth Lea, head of the Policy unit at the Institute of Directors.
"It does seem as though the economy is able to operate with slightly less spare capacity and not encounter wage inflation. But there's no room for complacency," she said.

Analysts argue that the "natural" jobless total, the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment which is known as the NAIRU, has probably fallen from around eight percent in the 1980s to five or six percent now.
"I think it's quite clear that in the U.S. and the UK the natural rate of unemployment has come down," said SBC- Warburg economist Darren Winder.
"What we are now waiting to see is whether that spreads to the rest of Europe although clearly they have not undergone the same process of supply side reform that we have."

Winder says the New Paradigm is within grasp, forecasting unemployment will fall to 3.5 percent in 1999 but with average earnings growth at no point straying over 5.0 percent for more than a short period of time.
This compares with a peak in average earnings growth, a crucial barometer of inflation pressures, of 10 percent in the late 1980s.
Data published on Wednesday suggest Britain may already have broken out of the old mould of low unemployment boosting wage claims which in turn fuel inflation.

The July seasonally adjusted unemployment benefit claimant count dipped to 5.5 percent with the level falling to 1.55 million, the lowest since September 1980. But June average earnings data remained at 4.25 percent.
This combination bodes well for the British authorities, battling to extricate the country from the cycle of boom and bust which has afflicted it since the 1960s.
Analysts say that careful economic management is likely to be crucial over the next few months with the economy currently in the throes of a mini-boom, fuelled by rampant consumer demand.
But there is a strong chance it can avoid the wage/price spiral which caused inflation to soar to nearly 11.0 percent in the late 1980s boom.
Then the authorities imposed painfully high interest rates of 15 percent -- more than twice their 7.0 percent level now -- and sparked the longest recession since World War II.
Analysts are hopeful that the Bank of England's current "stitch in time" approach of regular 1/4 point interest rate rises could help avoid the policy mistakes of the past.

"What matters is that the Bank must stay ahead of the curve to make sure we approach equilibrium on growth and unemployment steadily," said Brian Henry, economics professor at the London Business School and ex-official at both the UK central bank and the International Monetary Fund.

British interest rates have risen in each of the past four months and the central bank, which took over conduct of monetary policy in May, has now announced a hiatus while it assesses the impact of the rate increases so far.

Henry argues that it was the speed at which British unemployment fell in the 1980s boom years which allowed inflation pressures to surge rather than that the absolute level of unemployment itself and says that is the main concern now.
